q: What is an Artificial Neural Network (ANN)?
options: A relational database system optimized for graph queries.
A computational model inspired by biological nervous systems, consisting of interconnected layers of nodes that process data.
A deterministic search algorithm that traverses binary trees using depth-first search.
A hardware processor designed exclusively for quantum parallel computing.

q: What is the core objective of the Q-learning algorithm in Reinforcement Learning?
options: To cluster unlabelled continuous state vectors using Euclidean distance.
To compute the maximum likelihood of transition probabilities in a partially observable environment.
To learn an optimal action-value function that estimates the expected total future reward for taking an action in a given state.
To eliminate all exploration and strictly follow a predefined heuristic policy.

q: What is the primary role of an Activation Function in a neural network?
options: To introduce non-linearity into the network, enabling it to learn complex non-linear mappings.
To speed up gradient descent by setting the learning rate to zero when error is high.
To automatically split training data into cross-validation folds.
To convert discrete text tokens into continuous floating-point vectors.

q: In an artificial neuron (Perceptron), what is the mathematical operation performed on the inputs (\(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\)) with weights (\(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n\)) and bias b before applying the activation function?
options: \(\max(w_1 x_1, \dots, w_n x_n) + b\)

q: What does overfitting mean in machine learning?
options: The model performs exceptionally well on the training data but fails to generalize to unseen test data.
The model is too simple to capture the underlying trend in both training and test data.
The model takes too long to converge due to an excessively small learning rate.
The loss function reaches a local saddle point where all gradients evaluate to zero.

q: In natural gradient descent, parameter updates are performed along the steepest descent direction invariant to reparameterization. Which matrix is used to define the Riemannian metric manifold for this optimization?
options: The Hessian matrix of the empirical risk \(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L}(\theta\)).
The Fisher Information Matrix \(F = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta(x,y)}\left[\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x,y) \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x,y)^T\right]\).
The uncentered covariance matrix of input activations across all layers.
The Gram matrix of the feature vectors computed in reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS).

q: Why does AdamW decouple weight decay from the gradient update step, unlike traditional \(L_2\) regularization in standard Adam?
options: Because \(L_2\) regularization in Adam causes the second moment estimate \(v_t\) to scale proportionally with weight decay gradients, inadvertently penalizing weights with historically large gradients less than weights with small gradients.
Because \(L_2\) regularization introduces non-differentiable points at the origin that break momentum accumulation.
Because standard Adam computes weight updates exclusively in fp16 precision where gradient addition underflows.
Because decoupled decay guarantees that the spectral norm of the weight matrices remains strictly bounded by \(\le 1\).

q: In the FlashAttention algorithm (Dao et al.), how is exact standard self-attention computed with significantly reduced wall-clock time and memory footprint?
options: By projecting Q and K into low-rank representations using random Fourier features.

By tiling inputs into SRAM blocks and computing the softmax incrementally using online softmax normalization, avoiding reading/writing the \(N \times N\) attention matrix to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).
By quantizing intermediate attention weights to 4-bit integers and pruning attention heads with low entropy.
By swapping outer-product matrix multiplications with fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms in the frequency domain.

q: In Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), how is the explicit reward model \(r_\psi(x, y\)) from RLHF bypassed during policy optimization?
options: By training an actor-critic network where the critic updates solely on self-supervised masked tokens.

By analytically reparameterizing the ground-truth reward function as a closed-form function of the policy \(\pi_\theta(y|x\)) and reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x\)), substituting it directly into the Bradley-Terry preference loss.
By replacing cross-entropy loss with an optimal transport Earth Mover's Distance between chosen and rejected sequences.
By running Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) over the vocabulary during token generation to prune non-preferred trajectories.

q: In Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM), what is the theoretical relationship between the score function \(\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t\)) and the noise prediction network \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t\))?
options: \(\nabla_{x_t} \log q_t(x_t) = -\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}}\)
\(\nabla_{x_t} \log q_t(x_t) = \frac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}}\)
\(\nabla_{x_t} \log q_t(x_t) = -\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \cdot \beta_t^2\)
\(\nabla_{x_t} \log q_t(x_t) = \left( \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \right)^T \left( x_t - \mu_t \right)\)

q: In Statistical Learning Theory, what does the Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) Dimension of a hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) measure?
options: The maximum number of training samples a model can store in active memory without paging to disk.
The size of the largest finite set of points that can be shattered by \(\mathcal{H}\) (i.e., assigned all possible \(2^N\) binary label combinations).
The expected \(L_1\) Lipschitz constant of the loss landscape with respect to parameter perturbation.
The exact minimum number of epochs required for empirical risk minimization to achieve zero generalization error.

q: In the infinite-width limit under specific initialization scaling, what happens to an artificial neural network according to the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory?
options: The network degenerates into a linear logistic regression model with zero capacity.
The empirical NTK stays constant throughout gradient flow training, making network training analytically equivalent to kernel regression with a fixed deterministic kernel.
The Fisher Information Matrix becomes singular, halting all gradient propagation regardless of depth.
The activations collapse into a deterministic chaos regime characterized by positive Lyapunov exponents.

q: What is the theoretical upper limit on the expressive power of standard Message Passing Graph Neural Networks (MPNNs) in distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs?
options: They can distinguish any pair of non-isomorphic planar graphs with probability \(1\).
They are at most as powerful as the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) graph isomorphism test.
They are strictly equivalent to the 3-WL test if sum-aggregation is used.
Their expressive capacity is bounded only by the rank of the adjacency matrix Laplacian spectrum.

q: In Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), how is relative position information injected into the Query (q) and Key (k) vector inner product?
options: By adding a learned position embedding tensor directly to the attention logit matrix: \(A_{ij} = q_i^T k_j + b_{i-j}\).

By rotating 2D slices of the vectors in the complex plane such that \(\langle R_{\Theta, m}^d q, R_{\Theta, n}^d k \rangle = g(q, k, m - n\)), making the inner product dependent solely on relative distance (m - n).
By projecting input embeddings through a continuous sinusoidal Fourier shift operator prior to multi-head projection.
By masking the attention matrix with a static Cauchy matrix parameterizing token indices.

q: In the InfoNCE loss used in contrastive representation learning (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\mathbb{E}\left[\log \frac{\exp(s(x, x^+)/\tau)}{\exp(s(x, x^+)/\tau) + \sum_{j} \exp(s(x, x^-_j)/\tau)}\right]\)), minimizing this loss is mathematically equivalent to maximizing:
options: A lower bound on the Mutual Information I(X; Y) between positive views.
The Rényi divergence between negative sampling distributions.
The Wasserstein-1 distance across distinct batch instances.
An upper bound on the cross-entropy of latent cluster assignments.

q: In Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE), what is the effect of tuning the hyperparameter \(\lambda \in [0, 1\)] in \(\text{GAE}(\gamma, \lambda\))?
options: \(\lambda = 0\) yields maximum variance and zero bias (pure Monte Carlo return); \(\lambda = 1\) yields lowest variance and highest bias.
\(\lambda = 0\) corresponds to the standard 1-step TD advantage (lowest variance, highest bias); \(\lambda = 1\) corresponds to the empirical Monte Carlo advantage (highest variance, lowest bias).
\(\lambda\) controls the entropy regularization penalty added to the policy objective.
\(\lambda\) scales the clipping threshold in the surrogate PPO objective function.

q: In the Double Descent phenomenon observed in deep learning models, what happens to the test risk around the interpolation threshold (where model capacity matches sample size)?
options: The test risk drops asymptotically to zero.
The test risk peaks sharply because the empirical data covariance matrix is poorly conditioned, leading to exploding norm of the minimum-norm interpolating parameters.
The model transitions instantly into the underfitting regime where training error diverges.
The Hessian becomes positive definite, preventing SGD from traversing saddle points.

q: In Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), why is the weight update parameterized as \(\Delta W = B \cdot A\) (where \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}, B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}\) with \(r \ll \min(d, k\))), and how are A and B initialized?
options: A and B are both initialized from a Gaussian distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1\)) to promote exploration of rank space.
A is initialized from Gaussian distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2\)) and B is initialized to zero, ensuring \(\Delta W = 0\) at the start of training.
Both A and B are initialized as identity matrices to preserve pre-trained feature mappings.
B is initialized as an orthogonal matrix via QR decomposition and A is set to zero.

q: In Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), what is the "posterior collapse" phenomenon and what causes it?
options: The encoder collapses all latent variables to \(\infty\), causing floating point overflows in the decoder.
The approximate posterior \(q_\phi(z|x\)) matches the prior p(z) completely, causing the decoder to ignore the latent code z because the autoregressive decoder is expressive enough on its own.
The variance of the decoder's Gaussian likelihood collapses to \(0\), turning ELBO into an ill-posed deterministic reconstruction.
The gradient of the KL-divergence term dominates the reconstruction loss, forcing weights to undergo numerical underflow.

q: In state space models like Mamba (S6), how does the Selective State Space mechanism overcome the fundamental linear time-invariant (LTI) restriction of predecessor models like S4?
options: By replacing ODE solvers with an attention matrix computation over chunked sub-sequences.

By making the discretization step size \(\Delta\) and transition parameters (B, C) input-dependent functions of the current token \(x_t\), processed in linear time via a hardware-aware parallel associative scan.
By substituting the continuous convolution operation with an auto-regressive multi-layer perceptron.
By dynamically masking the state matrix A to retain only top-k eigenvalues.

q: Why does RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Normalization) replace standard Layer Normalization in architectures like LLaMA and Mistral?
options: RMSNorm enforces exact unit mean and zero variance, completely eliminating shift bias.
RMSNorm drops the mean-centering operation, calculating scaling exclusively based on root mean square of activations, which reduces computational overhead without degrading downstream performance.
RMSNorm operates across the sequence dimension instead of the hidden channel dimension, speeding up GEMM operations.
RMSNorm guarantees the Jacobian of the residual stream has singular values strictly equal to \(1\).

q: In the context of generative diffusion models, what is the key difference between using Deterministic DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models) and Stochastic DDPM during sampling?
options: DDIM reformulates the generative process as the discretization of an equivalent continuous ordinary differential equation (ODE), allowing deterministic sampling in significantly fewer steps with fixed initial noise.
DDIM discards the reverse noise schedule and evaluates the model exclusively in the frequency domain.
DDIM requires fine-tuning the model using a classification-guided policy gradient rather than standard MSE.
DDIM trains a secondary discriminator network to replace iterative reverse Langevin dynamics.

q: In Mixture of Experts (MoE) routing (e.g., in Mixtral / Switch Transformer), why is an auxiliary load-balancing loss added to the training objective?
options: To force the router logits to sum to exactly \(1\) without running a softmax.
To prevent "router collapse" where the gating network repeatedly selects the same small subset of preferred experts, leaving the remaining experts untrained and starved of gradients.
To penalize experts whose weight tensors have large spectral radii.
To synchronize the gradients of parallel GPUs during all-to-all communication primitives.

q: In Continuous Normalizing Flows and Flow Matching, what is the primary advantage of training models with Optimal Transport (OT) displacement interpolation over standard diffusion trajectories?
options: OT paths define straight-line probability trajectories in state space with constant vector fields, leading to faster ODE integration during inference with fewer function evaluations (NFE).
OT guarantees that the generative density is strictly multimodal without requiring score matching.
OT eliminates the need for computing the trace of the Jacobian matrix during likelihood computation.
OT allows arbitrary non-differentiable target distributions to be mapped into the latent prior.

q: Consider a distribution-free supervised learning setup with bounded loss. According to the PAC-Bayes Theorem (McAllester's bound), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over the draw of training set S of size m, for any posterior distribution Q over the hypothesis space: What quantity upper-bounds the true generalization risk \(\mathcal{R}(Q\)) relative to empirical risk \(\hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(Q\))?
options: \(\mathcal{R}(Q) \le \hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(Q) + \sqrt{\frac{\text{KL}(Q \parallel P) + \ln(2\sqrt{m}/\delta)}{2m}}\) (where P is the prior chosen independently of S).
\(\mathcal{R}(Q) \le \hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(Q) + \frac{\text{VC-Dim}(\mathcal{H})}{m} \ln\left(\frac{m}{\delta}\right)\).
\(\mathcal{R}(Q) \le \hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(Q) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}} \sum_{i=1}^m \mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[\sigma_i f(x_i\))].
\(\mathcal{R}(Q) \le \hat{\mathcal{R}}_S(Q) + \left( \frac{\text{Tr}(F^{-1})}{m} \right) \ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\).
